analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card late fees at $8 and limits them to issuers' actual costs.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card late fees at $8 was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on January 15, 2026 and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill caps the late fee a large credit card company can charge at $8 and says the fee cannot exceed what a late payment actually costs the company. It would write a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau late-fee rule into federal law so the limit is set by Congress rather than resting on a regulation that can be reversed in court. Since its referral to the Senate Banking Committee, the bill has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that get hit with credit card late fees, especially people who carry balances and pay late occasionally. The $8 cap replaces fees that frequently run $30 or more, and the bill also bars large issuers from charging more than the late payment actually costs them, so fees stop being a profit source. The cap applies only to issuers with 1 million or more open accounts, so it targets the biggest card companies rather than small banks and credit unions.

how_it_helps.text: Caps late fees charged by large card issuers — those with 1 million or more open accounts — at $8 per late payment, where fees today often run $30 or more.
Bars large issuers from charging late fees in excess of their actual cost from the late payment, so fees cannot contribute to issuer profits.
Lets the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau raise the cap over time, but only by the rate of inflation, so the limit cannot be quietly eroded.
Requires the CFPB to publicly release the research behind any rule it writes under the bill before the comment period, and channels any court challenge to the D.C. federal district court.

analysis.who_pays: Large credit card issuers — banks and card companies with 1 million or more open accounts — which would lose late-fee revenue that is currently a major profit source on card portfolios. The bill's stated purpose is precisely to limit fees to an amount 'reasonable and proportional' with issuer costs.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies only to issuers with 1 million or more open accounts; smaller banks and credit unions can still charge whatever their card agreements allow, so relief is uneven.

The bill sets the $8 figure directly and lets the CFPB raise it only with inflation, so if the cost of collecting a late payment rises faster than prices, the cap could fall below issuers' real costs — critics of the underlying rule argued issuers would then recoup the money through higher interest rates, annual fees, or tighter credit for riskier borrowers, effects the bill does not address.
The bill changes the statute to consider only the creditor's cost from the late payment, removing the broader factors regulators previously considered when judging whether a fee is fair.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cardholders who occasionally pay late, the savings are real and immediate: an $8 cap instead of fees that commonly reach $30 or more, with the fee tied to the issuer's actual cost. The cost falls on a concentrated group — the largest card-issuing banks — whose late-fee revenue would shrink. The main design weaknesses are the exemption for smaller issuers and the fact that issuers can shift revenue to interest rates and other charges the bill does not touch. On balance, the direct effect favors cardholders over issuers, and the bill's own stated purpose is to lock in a consumer-protection rule it says was properly issued.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the session so far.

narrative.text: Senator John Fetterman introduced the Credit Card Fairness Act on January 15, 2026, with Senators Booker and Baldwin joining at introduction; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
Five Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
Since the referral, the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

The bill's purpose section says it is meant to codify the CFPB's late-fee rule under Regulation Z, which capped late fees at $8 before being challenged in court; writing the limit into statute would put it beyond that kind of legal reversal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large credit card issuers are better off so far: with the bill stuck in committee, they keep collecting late fees at current levels and cardholders get no relief. If it stays parked, the industry keeps that revenue for the rest of this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large credit card issuers, so far

for.name: John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Senate Banking Committee.

for.name: Cory Booker and Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

against.name: Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without action since its January 2026 referral.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Fought the underlying CFPB late-fee cap in court and in public comments, and oppose writing it into statute; late fees are a major revenue source for large card issuers.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred, but the sponsorship is entirely Democratic — 5 of 45 Senate Democrats — with no Republican cosponsors, in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats and control the committee calendar.

industries.industry: Large credit card issuers (banks with 1M+ card accounts)
industries.note: The bill caps their late fees at $8 and bars fees above the actual cost of a late payment, cutting a revenue stream that currently runs well past what late payments cost issuers. Cardholders who pay late would keep that difference in their pockets.

Issuers with fewer than 1 million open accounts are exempt from the cap, so they could keep charging higher late fees while their large competitors are limited — a competitive edge, but at cardholders' expense.

analysis.trajectory: With 5 of 45 Senate Democrats cosponsoring, no Republican support, and no action since its January 2026 referral to the Senate Banking Committee, the bill is likely to sit without a markup or vote and expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. A late-fee cap could still be pursued through the regulatory route the bill is trying to replace.
